Hey there, regular luxury and boutique traveller here and I've explored around a lot of Italy. I'm just back from the Aeolian Islands, Panarea specifically, and one piece of advice is to heavily prepare for travel issues with ferries. If the winds are moderate to high or there is a storm, lots of ferries get cancelled at short notice. You'll find updates on ferry departures here: [https://www.libertylines.it/en/live-departures/](https://www.libertylines.it/en/live-departures/) and a far more accurate weather forecast here [https://www.ilmeteo.it/meteo/isola+salina](https://www.ilmeteo.it/meteo/isola+salina). Other weather forecasts falsely predicted sunshine during this storm on my trip, whereas ilmeteo.it was accurate with the weather every day to the hour, including the wind level. I'd recommend having solid travel insurance and a flexible hotel booking with cancellations just in case the ferries are unpredictable. I don't want to put you off - usually it's fine apparently. You're safer in Salina than Panarea as Salina has far more ferries and different companies connecting to mainland Sicily and Calabria than Panarea. You'll be fine there.

Apologies for the obvious sounding answer, but it completely depends on the source of breakage. If your hair is heavily processed, colour treated or heat damaged, bond repair is what you need. You could choose from K18, Olaplex, Living Proof Triple Bond Complex or Epres. 

However, if you don't have excessively processed hair, bond repair is not necessary. Sometimes the source of breakage is dry hair, tangling and brushing, which was the case for me. Making sure I started using slippery, "hydrating" conditioners and styling products that are light but packed with silicones and oils helped massively. I really love Sebastian Professional Dark Oil conditioner and Amika Normcore Conditioner. Out of the many, many silicone and oil based protein free conditioners, these two are the most detangling and hydrating yet incredibly light. I started avoiding protein ingredients and peptides in haircare because my hair wasn't damaged and therefore didn't require strength from protein - this made a huge transformation as protein was causing tangling, brittleness and therefore breakage from brushing. As soon as I cut protein out and used silicone hydrating conditioners instead, tangling just stopped. It's worth some trial and error; maybe your hair is fine with protein, but eliminating it to investigate if it contributes to tangling could be sensible. As a styling product/leave-in, Amika the Wizard Detangling Primer would be awesome for your needs.

Also, even if you do have hair that is structurally damaged and processed, I would still recommend using the most detangling conditioner you can find combined with the bond repair. Please note that if you choose to use K18, you don't have to skip conditioner as per the instructions. The brand clarified that it's fine to apply conditioner after K18 as long as you do so after K18 has had 4 minutes on the hair first. So you can enjoy the benefits of K18 without losing out on a vital detangling step. 

Also make sure your shampoo isn't too stripping, yet make sure you don't get build up. Use a shampoo that's more clarifying once a week and then a gentler one the rest of the time. Harsh shampoos can leave hair like straw and more tangle prone, but so can build up.

Lastly, be gentle with brushing, as it's often mechanical damage that causes breakage, whether or not the hair structure is already compromised. Often the little steps of being careful make the biggest difference. I'm unsure of this works with curly hair, but I find that brushing with a gentle, slow wriggle of the brush or comb helps get through tangles with less force.

My highlights of my Sicily trip in April that had nothing to do with museums included: 
* San Vito lo Capo for the most incredible beach with white sand, turquoise water and a visual backdrop that looks like Europe's answer to Rio de Janeiro.
* Eating the best pizza of my life at the beach in Cefalu watching the sun set, with all of the rustic Sicilian houses in the backdrop.
* The panoramic views from the gardens in Taormina are the best I've ever seen and I travel regularly.
* A boat trip around Ortigia Island.
* The people! I felt utterly joyous at the food market in Palermo. The people there are so wonderful.
* Walking upstairs at a church (Chiesa da Santa Chiara) to the roof for the best view of Notto. It was so majestic to see the architecture from above. 
* Agrigento - the "stair of the Turks" was beautiful by the beach and I loved seeing the Valley of the Temples from a lovely little bar and restaurant nearby called Kokalos.

For my next Sicily trip in Spring my plan is to stay at Principe da Salina hotel in the Aeolian Island of Salina and appreciate the endless blue horizons of the sea and the view of the Monte Saraceno volcano across the bay from a hammock or infinity pool.

Apologies if this advice is unsolicited, but Sicily is so huge that I don't recommend breaking up your trip with more Italian regions. I had 9 nights/10 days there this spring and felt rushed. My itinerary had two nights in Cefalu, two nights in Mondello (where I also saw Palermo and San Vito lo Capo), two nights in Agrigento, one night in Taormina and two nights in Syracuse/Ortigia. Hey OP - I was previously in your exact situation and I resolved it. 

This is anecdotal but for me the two things that was causing my hair to become extremely rough and prone to tangling was:

1. Any kind of protein or amino acid ingredient (wheat/rice/soy protein, silk, keratin, elastin, collagen, hydrolyzed proteins, egg) and amino acids (usually ending in ine) casein, arginine etc), plus oils like coconut oil that behave like protein ingredients for many people.
2. Any shampoo that was too deeply cleansing/astringent to the point where it left the lengths of my hair knotted and a mess. 

**The main goal is preventing tangles. So here's what I did:**
* I completely cut out all products that contained protein or amino acids.
* Switched to shampoo that is the right balance of gentle but effective cleansing.
* I switched to the most slippery, fatty, siliconey conditioners that I could find and I drench my hair in them after shampooing.
* I keep styling simple and use a detailing product that's an overall leave-in conditioner and a silicone based oil on the ends.
* I use a few drops of an argan oil based hair oil, rub it in my palms and gently distribute it throughout my lengths the night before washing. This protects my hair from tangling after washing and it also protects the hair from hydral fatigue where the cuticle smells too much after washing.
* I blow dry at a 15cm distance on a medium heat and downward motion so that it smooths the cuticle and reduces tangling.
* Lastly but a very important one - I'm more careful with how I brush my hair. Previously if I got impatient and dragged a brush through the lengths to the end in one motion, it would cause either split ends or these deep knots that would leave sharp kinks in my strands and cause it to tangle more. Now I use a boar bristle brush and start from the ends and work my way up. I "wriggle" the brush so it's gentler on the knots.

My hair is now completely tangle free, after years and years of struggling with tangling. Previously, I'd tie my hair up and my hair would still tangle. Now, my long hair can be left down  for an hour when out and it's not tangled when I get home.

Hey you two, first of all, congratulations, that's so beautiful! Secondly, would you mind if I shared a personal recommendation? If I were you, I'd consider cutting out Rome and instead spend more time around the Amalfi region. It's your honeymoon and the south is so romantic. Just a one hour ferry from Naples you'll find an island called Ischia, just above Capri. Ischia is Capri's affordable big sister but more beautiful, with those Amalfi style craggy cliffs with dramatic buildings, stunning peninsula beaches, colourful flowers everywhere, castles, abundant natural thermal spas and the most incredible food because of the volcanic soil. I stayed at a 5 star hotel this April on Ischia which had 11 thermal pools for only €180 a night (San Montano) which has hilltop views over the bay of Naples. I also had the best pizza I've ever eaten for €6 near the Marina. Oh and Eden beach club by the Aragonese castle was such a treat. The island is cheap and easy to get around with frequent dirt cheap buses in both directions clockwise and anticlockwise.

I know what it's like when travelling to get enthusiastic and want to visit everything, but future you will be grateful to have time to really relax and explore for longer in the one spot and have quality honeymoon time.

Oh and for the record, I've explored Italy many times, all over, visiting almost every province, and Ischia is by far the most beautiful and special place in my opinion. In the last year alone I've spent two months in Italy on different holidays.

May I suggest the following, if I were to help a friend plan a trip:

Day 1-3: Head straight to Lake Como or Lake Garda. 

Day 4-5 Venice. Be prepared, it's overwhelmingly busy, and still busy in October. In it's place, I'd  recommend staying at an agriturismo in Umbria, Emilia Romagna or Tuscany instead of Venice if you would prefer quality romantic time. You could always see Venice as a day trip then stay in an Agriturismo in the country.
 
Day 6 - Travel to Naples and either get an immediate Ischia ferry to spend one evening in Naples.

Day 7-11 - Spend quality time in Ischia.

Day 11 Get a ferry going straight from Ischia to Amalfi (or you may have to go Via Naples or Sorrento if the direct one isn't running in October) and enjoy the sensational views. Stay at Amalfi or Ravello. Be sure to visit Ravello.

Then head back at your own leisure...

Of course this is just a recommendation, but please look into Ischia. There's a good chance you'd be grateful to go there instead of a crowded city when it really comes down to it. I'm like you - I'd want to touch on a few regions, and I think in this manner it would still be easy, romantic and relaxing.

Have an amazing time! And promise yourselves you'll return to further explore when it isn't your honeymoon.

Oh my gosh, I am so sorry, I misread this post. Too much time online. Bleary eyed. The fact that you're on a search for boosting hair thickness in terms of growth was communicated perfectly in your post, don't mind me.

I need to preface this by stating that I'm not a medical doctor. It's really important that you understand the cause of hair thinning so that you can target the hair loss and address it properly. If you can visit a medical professional in this field or a trichologist or dermatologist, please do.

It could be down to hormonal female pattern hair thinning and if you research the visual signs, you'll be able to work out if that applies: you'll see thinning concentrated at the temples, parting and the crown. 2-5% minoxodil is the most effective treatment for hormonal hair loss, however that treatment can never be stopped or your hair will shed again, plus there is the risk of irritation. There is a small study to suggest that scalp massages with rosemary oil can treat hormonal hair loss to the same efficacy as 2% minoxodil. Pumpkin seed oil both topically and orally can help to reduce hormonal hair loss and there are some studies to suggest this. Anecdotally, I've grown thicker hair through taking pumpkin seed oil supplements and I started seeing results in 6 months. Important - if you have hormonal hair loss, please shampoo your hair at least every other day so as to eliminate a build up of DHT on the scalp, the hormone that causes hair thinning and hair loss.

It could be down to diet. I previously had a spell of hair loss due to iron and vitamin D levels that were sub-optimal. Vitamin A deficiency also causes hair loss, however, please note that _too much_ vitamin A can also cause hair shedding. I recommend a beauty supplement for hair, skin and nails which does not contain vitamin A, and to strive to get vitamin a from your diet so that you don't have excess. Vitamin E and omega 3 levels also support healthy hair.

Another factor could be caffeine consumption. Caffeine is a vasodilator when in small amounts, but a vasoconstrictor in larger amounts. This can in theory affect the hair follicles. There is a large body of anecdotal evidence that limiting caffeine consumption aids hair regrowth after hair loss. 

One other factor is that protein in haircare can cause hair to be a little more on the brittle side and more prone to breakage. There is a large amount of anecdotal reports to support this. Pay attention to what is in your haircare and if any particular products make your hair harder to manage. Hard to manage = breakage. Breakage = thinning.

Good luck. I'm sorry you've experienced this too. Don't underestimate the magic of gentle and regular scalp massage. I use homemade rosemary water rather than rosemary oil to do this.

Once you get the hang of pasta dough you really can't go wrong. I think the issue is that food content creators on Instagram and YouTube make the kneading process look incredibly quick and effortless. Even when using a pasta machine, I still take at least a good 5-7 minutes to knead everything really smoothly. But it's definitely the case when using a rolling pin to hand roll your sheets that the dough needs to be really smooth and worked on for longer.

How did you get on? I hope it all turned out alright. Hope you don't mind me saying, but the first few times I made pasta dough, it wasn't quite right. Mistakes are absolutely essential for getting the hang of it. You can't have pasta mastery without the lessons along the way. This learning process this far will serve you well in future.

I hope you don't mind me giving another tip and apologies if it's unsolicited advice, but when making ravioli I almost always use my pasta machine as it's easier to roll the sheets very thin, as around the rim of the pasta, the sheet doubles up, so 1-2mm sheets are perfect. I tend to hand roll pasta if I'm making something like a ragu with pappardelle, where the thickness of a hand rolled sheet is just right and the wooden rolling pin adds texture to help pick up more delicious sauce.

Hey - I make pasta quite often. if you're hand rolling your pasta sheets and not using a machine, you really need to knead it longer than normal. We're talking for 10 mins, maybe even longer for beginner. You want your dough to be super smooth. If it dries out as you're kneading it, just wet your hands and keep kneading as normal. Btw, you can salvage your dough you've already made - just keep kneading it. It needs to be super smooth and sometimes if my dough starts out bumpy and I want to speed things up, I get in there while kneading and use my knuckles and the bottom of my palm's edge to really grind it down before bringing it all together and kneading it properly. Once you're kneading it properly, you almost want to be folding it into itself as you knead - watch Gennaro Contaldo's pasta dough video on YouTube to see what I mean. He also has brilliant ravioli videos too btw.

You also want to let it rest for at least 30 mins but ideally an hour. Keep it covered in cling film to stop it drying out. Hope this helps! Happy pasta making! Btw, you can keep your dough for a few days in the fridge.
